abstract: Understanding how distinct cell identities emerge from common progenitors requires access to regulatory histories that molecular snapshots cannot directly reveal. We introduce RegArch, a probabilistic framework integrating transcriptomic profiles, chromatin-derived evidence, and time-scaled cell lineages to reconstruct terminal and unobserved ancestral gene regulatory networks (GRNs). These lineage-resolved networks enable characterization of regulatory reorganization, prioritization of differentiation-associated and branch-biased regulators, and identification of constitutive, lineage-associated, and state-restricted modules. Simulations demonstrate ancestral network recovery and improved terminal GRN inference. In Caenorhabditis elegans, inferred ancestral GRNs combined with measured regulator expression generated target-expression signatures preferentially matching their corresponding progenitor profiles. EMS lineage analyses identified a shared regulatory module and branch-enriched modules with distinct ancestral representation. In zebrafish hearts sampled after injury, developmental ancestry informed endocardial- and epicardial-associated candidate regulator prioritization. RegArch thus generates testable hypotheses about the regulatory origins of cellular diversity.
